p.seg: Kǒngzǐ Jí Yǔ
Compiled by Xuē Jù of the Sòng dynasty.
Jù's courtesy name was Shūróng,
a native of Yǒngjiā.
He served as the Ever-Normal Granary Intendant of Eastern Zhè.
Lín Déyáng's "Collection from Mount Jì" contains a preface to the Collected Works of the Two Mr. Xuē, saying:
"The Xuē family's learning has spanned three hundred years.
Lord Yùchéng studied under Yáng Jìngzhòng of Lake Cí,
discarding the flowery and adhering to the substantial,
like the remaining strands from the school of the Chéng brothers.
When false learning flourished and was prohibited,
he single-handedly defended the Way,
He authored *Zhuó Yī Luò Yuán Liú*,
each forming a genealogy.
Furthermore, he imparted the methods of bow-making and metal-casting to his son, Gōng Shūróng,
whose ambitions were grand and whose strength was resolute,
bearing the burden of a thousand years.
Lamenting the distance from the sages and the obscurity of their words,
he compiled the *Kǒngzǐ Jí Yǔ* in twenty *juǎn* (scrolls/chapters),
which is this very book.
This edition only divides it into twenty sections,
comprising merely three *juǎn*.
Perhaps, in older times, one section was considered one *juǎn*,
which later generations combined.
The listed books number more than thirty.

Its general principles state that the four complete books, *Zēngzǐ*, *Dà Dài Lǐ*, *Kǒng Cóngzǐ*, and *Kǒngzǐ Jiā Yǔ*, as well as *Zuǒ Shì*, *Zhuāngzǐ*, *Xúnzǐ*, and *Lièzǐ*, are generally not adopted,
only those found in other ancient books are selected.
However, the *Kǒngzǐ Shìjiā* is listed in the official history,
not deviating from *Kǒng Cóng Jiā Yǔ*.
Moreover, it states that it will not include *Dà Dài Lǐ Jì*,
yet Yán Shūzǐ chapter twelve cites one passage from it,
contradicting its own rules.
Furthermore, it cites the *Shuōwén* on how millet can be used to make wine,
that grain enters the water,
that "one piercing through three" signifies a king,
and that "pushing one to combine with ten" signifies a *shì* (scholar), etc.,
combining several entries into one,
whose meanings are unrelated,
which is especially incoherent.
As for the *Hán Fēizǐ*, the chapters *Shuō Lín Xià*, *Nèi Chǔ Shuō Shàng*, *Nèi Chǔ Shuō Xià*, *Wài Chǔ Shuō Zuǒ Shàng*, *Wài Chǔ Shuō Yòu Xià*, *Nán Yī*, and *Nán Sān*,
There were twenty or so items that could be selected,
but this book only cites three.
For example, in the *Huáinánzǐ*, the chapters "Dào Yīng Xùn," "Zhǔ Shù Xùn," "Xià Qí Sú Xùn," "Xiū Wù Xùn," "Tài Sú Xùn," and "Yào Lüè,"
there are no fewer than ten items that could be selected,
but this only cites three as well.
Thus, the remaining omissions
can be generally understood.
Furthermore, Wén Xiángfèng's *Yún Mèng Yào Xī Tán*
extracts one item about "Wǔ Yǒu,"
citing *Sōushén Jì* while concealing its source,
and also mistakenly writes "Wǔ Yǒu" as "Wǔ Qiú."
Therefore, its mixed nature and errors
are also unavoidable.
However, it records many ancient Qin and Hàn books,
fragments and incomplete sentences,
which may be preserved only through this.
Therefore, those who study ancient texts cannot disregard it.
Preface
The *Kǒngzǐ Jíyǔ*
was compiled by Sūn Xīngyǎn of Yánghú, styled Bóyuān, who served as an observation commissioner.
Confucius elucidated the way of a hundred kings to instruct posterity.
Beyond the Six Classics,
the subtle words and profound meanings recorded in biographies and various schools of thought
are sufficient to aid the Classics and promote Confucian ideals,
and they often appear.
Among those compiled into books,
Emperor Wǔ of the Liáng dynasty's *Kǒngzǐ Zhèngyán* in twenty volumes and Wáng Bó's *Cì Lúnyǔ* in ten volumes
have not survived to the present day.
Extant are Yáng Jiǎn's 楊簡 *Xiānsheng Dàxùn* 《先聖大訓》 in ten volumes, Xuē Jù's 薛據 *Kǒngzǐ Jíyǔ* 《孔子集語》 in two volumes, and Pān Shìdá's 潘士達 *Lúnyǔ Wàipiān* 《論語外篇》 in twenty volumes.
Xuē's 薛 book is the most prominent,
but it inevitably has omissions and oversights.
Recently, Cáo Tíngdòng 曹廷棟
also compiled *Kǒngzǐ Yìyǔ* 《孔子逸語》 in ten volumes,
but his research was inaccurate and lacked verification,
so it is not worth discussing.
In the *xīnwèi* 辛未 year of the Jiāqìng 嘉慶 era
(1811), the *guānchá* 觀察 [official title, lit. "observer," often a provincial surveillance commissioner] retired from office due to illness.
Lamenting the deficiencies and omissions in Confucian texts,
he extensively searched through various books,
comprehensively verifying and comparing different versions.
He increased Xuē's 薛 book by six or seven times
but still named it *Kǒngzǐ Jíyǔ* 《孔子集語》;
this shows the principles behind his work.
The general rules for his compilation are as follows:

The *Yì Shíyì* 《易十翼》 (Ten Wings Commentary on the Book of Changes), *Lǐ Xiǎo Dàijì* 《禮小戴記》 (Record of Rituals by Dài the Younger), *Chūnqiū Zuǒshì Zhuàn* 《春秋左氏傳》 (Zuo Tradition Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals), *Xiàojīng* 《孝經》 (Classic of Filial Piety), *Lúnyǔ* 《論語》 (Analects), and *Mèngzǐ* 《孟子》 (Mencius)
are universally recited and studied,
so they are not included.
The *Jiāyǔ* 《家語》 (School Sayings of Confucius) and *Kǒng Cóngzǐ* 《孔叢子》 (Master Kong's Family Sayings)
are complete books that circulate independently,
so they are not included.
The "Kongzi Shijia" 孔子世家 (Hereditary House of Confucius) and "Dizi Zhuan" 弟子傳 (Biographies of Disciples) in the *Shǐjì* 《史記》 (Records of the Grand Historian)
are easy to find, so they are also not included.
As for the remaining commentaries on the Classics, apocryphal texts, various histories, and philosophical works,
as well as anthologies from the Tang and Song dynasties,
both lengthy passages and single sentences are fully recorded,
without selection or omission.
All clearly state the source of the passages, volume by volume.
In cases where there were suspected omissions or incomplete sentences,
appropriate annotations were added.
Some matters are mutually referenced in different places,
even appearing five or six times.
Strengths and weaknesses, merits and shortcomings,
can be mutually verified and understood.
After more than a year,
the initial draft was completed.
Two years later,
it was entrusted to his friend Yūchéng Yán Kějūn of Wūchéng,
who, roughly imitating the style of the *Shuō Yuàn* (Garden of Stories),
organized and oversaw it.
Re-examining many books,
correcting erroneous characters,
rearranging the order,
adding to what was missing,
resulted in fourteen chapters:
"Exhortation to Learning" (Quàn Xué) being the first,
"The Foundation of Filial Piety" (Xiào Běn) the second,
"The Five Natures" (Wǔ Xìng) the third,
"The Six Arts" (Liù Yì) the fourth,
"The Virtue of the Ruler" (Zhǔ Dé) the fifth,
"The Art of the Minister" (Chén Shù) the sixth,
"The Way of Association" (Jiāo Dào) the seventh,
"On People" (Lùn Rén) the eighth,
"On Governance" (Lùn Zhèng) the ninth,
"Natural History" (Bówù) the tenth,
Chapter Eleven: Records of Affairs,
Chapter Twelve: Miscellaneous Matters,
Chapter Thirteen: Extant Prophecies,
Chapter Fourteen: Allegories.
Each chapter is a scroll;
the scrolls of the Six Arts, Records of Affairs, and Allegories are large,
and are divided into upper and lower sections,
making seventeen scrolls out of fourteen chapters.
Chapters such as "Exhortation to Learning"
are closely related to the main text.
The Extant Prophecies are not pure,
the Allegories are likely based on conjecture.
It was then printed in Jīnlíng
and made public to later generations.
-- Preface by Yán Kějūn.
Memorial
Sūn Xīngyǎn, your subject, Commissioner of Grain Transport for Shāndōng, kowtows and respectfully submits this memorial, saying,
your subject's completed *Kǒngzǐ Jíyǔ* (Collected Sayings of Confucius) in fourteen chapters,
I respectfully present it in this memorial for your consideration.
Humbly, Huáng Zhuān transmitted the Dao,
and the Vermillion Book was prepared with the ceremony of facing north;
the River Chart and Luo River Writing emerged,
and Yuánhù had the custom of an eastern tour.
To reconcile diverse opinions, one awaits the ultimate sage,
and examining the ancients is how one aligns with Heaven.
I respectfully reflect that our Emperor elegantly praises the classics,
and venerates the Sage in the Imperial Academy.
As vast as Heaven,
Yáo's essence is hard to name;
like the sun diligently shining,
Yǔ thought of listening to good advice.
What is gathered from the grass and firewood is indispensable;
moreover, instructions and guidance have clear evidence.
In the past, Confucius,
Attached to the Duke of Qūelǐ,
Recounting the ancestral virtue of the Sage's school.
Respectfully presented for Your Majesty's perusal,
May it serve as an aid at your side,
Widely disseminated throughout the Confucian community,
And humbly compared to the texts found in the wall.
Your subject is overcome with trepidation and awe,
Gazing at the heavens and longing for the imperial palace,
Leaping with joy and elation.
Respectfully presented through Yǎnshèng Gōng, your subject Qìngróng,
Submitting this memorial to Your Majesty for your kind attention.

Exhortation to Learning 1
*Shàngshū Dàzhuàn · Lüèshuō* (Commentary on the Book of Documents - Abridged Explanation) Confucius said:
“A *jūnzǐ* (gentleman) cannot but learn;
when seeing others, one cannot but be presentable.
Without being presentable, there is no proper appearance;
without proper appearance, there is no respect;
without respect, there are no rites;
without rites, one cannot be established.
That which shines from afar
is being presentable;
that which becomes brighter upon closer inspection
is learning.
It is like a ditch;
collected floodwaters gather there,
and rushes and reeds grow.
When viewed from above,
who would know that it is not spring water!"
*Dà Dài Lǐ · Quàn Xué* (The Great Dai Ritual - Exhortation to Learning) Confucius said:
"How uncultivated!
A *jūnzǐ* cannot but learn;
when seeing others, one cannot but be adorned.
Without adornment, there is no proper appearance;
without proper appearance, there is no respect;
without respect, there are no rites;
without rites, one cannot be established.
That which shines from afar
is adornment;
That which, being near, becomes even brighter,
is learning.
It is like a dirty and foul place
where accumulated rainwater gathers,
and rushes and cattails grow.
Viewing it from above,
who would know that it is not a spring!"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Lǐ,
a gentleman must not fail to learn,
and when seeing people, must not fail to adorn himself.
If he does not adorn himself, he will have no root;
if he has no root, he will lose principle;
if he loses principle, he will be disloyal;
if he is disloyal, he will lose ritual propriety;
if he loses ritual propriety, he will not be able to stand.
That which, being distant, has light,
is adornment;
that which, being near, becomes even brighter,
is learning.
It is like a dirty pond
where accumulated rainwater flows,
and *jiān* rushes and cattails grow.
Viewing it from above,
one knows that it is not a spring."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"A gentleman has three worries:
not knowing,
Can one be without worry?
Knowing but not learning,
Can one be without worry?
Learning but not practicing,
Can one be without worry?"
*Hán Shī Wài Zhuàn* Six. Zǐ Yuē (Confucius said):
"To not learn but to like thinking,
though one knows, it will not be extensive;
to learn but be negligent in self-cultivation,
though one learns, one will not be respected;
to not establish oneself with sincerity,
though one stands, it will not be for long;
if sincerity is not manifested but one likes to speak,
though one speaks, it will not be believed.
A beautiful talent,
but not hearing the Dào of the Jūnzǐ.
Concealing small things to harm great things,
calamity will surely befall oneself."
*Hán Shī Wài Zhuàn* Six. Kǒngzǐ said:
"Those with whom one can talk all day without weariness,
it is only through learning!
Their physical body is not worth looking at,
their courage and strength are not worth fearing,
their clan name is not worth mentioning,
their ancestors are not worth talking about,
but they can be heard in all directions and known among the lords,
it is only through learning!"
*Shuō Yuàn · Jiàn Běn*. Kǒngzǐ said:
"That which allows one to spend the entire day with others without fatigue,
is perhaps only learning!
One's physical appearance is not worth admiring,
one's courage and strength are not worth fearing,
one's ancestors are not worth praising,
one's clan name is not worth mentioning,
yet one can open up the four quarters and become well-known among the various lords;
it is perhaps only learning!"
*Hán Shī Wài Zhuàn*, chapter eight. Kǒngzǐ was relaxing in his leisure when
Zǐgòng adjusted his clothes and stepped forward, saying:
"Your disciple has served you, Master, for many years.
My talent is exhausted and my wisdom fatigued.
I exert myself in learning,
but I dare not advance further.
I beg for a rest."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Where do you, Cì, wish to rest?" He said:
"I wish to rest from serving a ruler."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The *Shī* says:
'From early morning until late at night, without negligence,
to serve one person.'
To do it like this
is not easy.
How can you rest!" He said:
"I wish to rest from serving my parents."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The *Shī* says:
“A filial son is never lacking,
And will forever be blessed with your kind.”
To achieve this state is
not easy.
How can one find rest?" Zì Gòng said,
"Cì wishes to find rest in serving his brothers."
Kǒngzǐ said,
"The *Shī* says,
'Wife and children in good accord,
Like playing the sè and qín.
When brothers are united,
They are harmonious, happy, and content.'
To achieve this state is
not easy.
How can one find rest?" Zì Gòng said,
"Cì wishes to find rest in farming."
Kǒngzǐ said,
"The *Shī* says,
'By day, you gather thatch;
By night, you twist rope.
Quickly you climb the roof,
And then you begin to sow all the grains.'
To achieve this state is
not easy.
How can one find rest?"
Zǐ Gòng said,
"Does the junzi ever rest?"
Kǒngzǐ said,
"Only when the coffin is closed does the sowing cease,
unaware that time easily passes.
This is what is called the gentleman's rest."
*Xúnzǐ · Dàlüè*: Zǐgòng asked Kǒngzǐ,
"Sì is weary of learning
and wishes to cease serving the ruler."
Kǒngzǐ said,
"The *Shī* says,
'Be gentle and respectful morning and night,
perform your duties with diligence.'
Serving a ruler is difficult,
how can serving a ruler be ceased!"
"Then Sì wishes to cease serving his parents."
Kǒngzǐ said,
"The *Shī* says,
'A filial son is never deficient,
may you always receive blessings.'
Serving parents is difficult,
how can serving parents be ceased!"
"Then Sì wishes to rest with his wife and children."
Kǒngzǐ said,
"The *Shī* says,
'Model yourself on your wife,
extend it to your brothers,
and so govern your family and state.'
Wife and children are difficult,
how can wife and children be ceased!"
"Then Sì wishes to rest with friends."
Confucius said:
"The *Shī* (*Book of Poetry*) says:
'Friends are there to help each other,
Help each other with dignified manners.'
Being a friend is difficult,
How can one rest from being a friend!"
"Then, Cì wishes to rest from farming."
Confucius said:
"The *Shī* (*Book of Poetry*) says:
'In the day you gather thatch,
At night you twist rope,
Hasten to roof the house,
Then begin to sow all the grains.'
Farming is difficult,
How can one rest from farming!"
"Then, is there nothing from which Cì can rest?"
Confucius said:
"Look at the grave;
It is a mound,
It is filled,
It is separated;
Then you will know where to rest."
Zǐgòng said:
"Great is death!
The gentleman rests there,
The common man finds respite there."
*Lièzǐ · Tiānruì* Zǐgòng was weary of learning
and said to Zhòngní:
“I wish to have rest.”
Zhòng Ní said:
“In life, there is no rest.”
Zǐ Gòng said:
“Then does Cì have no place to rest?”
Zhòng Ní said:
“There is a place!
Look at his tomb,
broad like this,
enclosed like this,
mounded like this,
separated like this,
then you know where to rest.”
Zǐ Gòng said:
“Great is death!
The gentleman rests there,
the small man is buried there.”
Zhòng Ní said:
“Cì,
you understand it.
People all know the joy of life,
but do not know the bitterness of life;
know the weariness of old age,
but do not know the ease of old age;
know the evil of death,
but do not know the rest of death.”
*Dà Dài Lǐ · Quàn Xué* Confucius said:
"I once spent the whole day thinking,
It's better to study for even a short while;
I have tried standing on tiptoe to look at it,
It's not as good as climbing high to see broadly.
Climbing high and waving,
It's not that one's arm is long,
Yet what is seen is far away;
Shouting with the wind,
It's not that the voice is louder,
Yet what is heard is distinct.
One who uses carriages and horses,
It's not that their feet are swift,
Yet they reach a thousand *lǐ*;
One who uses boats and oars,
It's not that they are good at swimming,
Yet they cross rivers and seas.
The nature of the *jūnzǐ*,
Is not different,
But they are good at making use of things."
*Xúnzǐ*, *Yòuzuò* Confucius said:
"I have things I am ashamed of,
I have things I despise,
I have things I worry about.
When young, not being able to strive to learn,
When old, having nothing to teach,
I am ashamed of this;
Leaving one's hometown,
Serving a ruler and becoming successful,
Eventually encountering an old friend,
"If someone has no regard for the sayings of the past,
I despise him.
If someone associates with petty people,
I am wary of him."
*Xúnzǐ · Yòuzuò* Kǒngzǐ said:
"If one advances like an ant hill,
I will support him.
If one stops like a hill,
I will cease my support."
Nowadays, learning has not even reached the level of a wart or wen,
yet people presumptuously desire to be teachers.
*Xúnzǐ · Yòuzuò* Zǐgòng observed the northern hall of the Lǔ temple,
came out, and asked Kǒngzǐ,
"Just now,
I, Cì, observed the northern hall of the Grand Temple.
I did not stop looking,
and kept repeatedly gazing at the nine canopies, all of which were joined together.
Is there an explanation for this?
Did the craftsmen overdo it?"
Kǒngzǐ said,
"The hall of the Grand Temple once had an explanation.
Officials hired skilled craftsmen,
who added beautiful details and ornamentation.
It's not that there was a lack of good materials,
but rather, the emphasis was on refined decoration."
*Xúnzǐ · Zǐdào* Zǐlù asked Kǒngzǐ,
"Does a *jūnzǐ* also have worries?"
Kǒngzǐ said,
"The superior man,
when he has not yet attained something,
delights in the intention of it;
once he has attained it,
he delights in its management.
Therefore, he has lifelong joy,
without a single day of sorrow.
The petty man,
when he has not yet attained something,
worries about not attaining it;
once he has attained it,
he fears losing it.
Therefore, he has lifelong sorrow,
without a single day of joy."
*Shuō Yuàn · Zá Yán* Zǐlù asked Kǒngzǐ, saying:
"Does the superior man also have worries?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"No.
The superior man cultivates his conduct;
before attaining something,
he delights in the intention of it;
once he has attained it,
he delights in understanding it.
Therefore, he has lifelong joy,
without a single day of sorrow.
The petty man is not like this;
before attaining something,
he worries about not attaining it;
Having already obtained it,
one then fears losing it.
Therefore, one has worries all day long,
without a single day of joy."
*Xúnzǐ, Fǎ Xíng* Kǒngzǐ said:
"The junzi has three considerations
that one cannot but consider:
If young and not learning,
when grown, one will be incapable.
If old and not teaching,
upon death, one will not be remembered.
If possessing and not giving,
when impoverished, one will have no helpers.
Therefore, the junzi, when young, considers being grown and then learns;
when old, considers death and then teaches;
when possessing, considers poverty and then gives."
*Yù Lǎn* 607 quotes *Shènzǐ* Kǒngzǐ said:
"Qiū was fond of learning when young
and heard the Dao later in life.
This is how I became broad in knowledge."
*Qúnshū Zhìyào,* *Shīzǐ · Quàn Xué* Fūzǐ said:
"For a carriage,
one only fears the ground not being solid; for a boat,
one only fears the water not being deep.
If one possesses the tools,
then one can turn what is difficult for people into what is easy.
Now the Dao
turns what is difficult for people into what is easy."
*Qún Shū Zhì Yào*, *Shī Zǐ*·*Chǔ Dào*: Confucius said:
"If you wish to know, then ask;
if you wish to be capable, then learn;
if you wish to be sufficient, then prepare beforehand;
if you wish to be good, then practice diligently.
If the state is in turmoil, then select the wicked people and remove them,
then the state will be governed well;
if one's heart is in turmoil,
then select the wicked desires and cast them away,
then virtue will be rectified."
*Yì Lín* quotes *Shī Zǐ*: Confucius said:
"Reciting poetry and reading books is
to dwell with the ancients;
reading books and reciting poetry is
to deliberate with the ancients."
*Zhuāng Zǐ*·*Zá Piān*·*Ràng Wáng*: Confucius said to Yán Huí:
"Huí! Come here.
Your family is poor and your dwelling is humble,
why don't you take office?"
Yán Huí replied:
"I do not wish to take office.
Huí has fifty *mǔ* of fields outside the city,
enough to provide thin gruel;
ten *mǔ* of fields inside the city,
enough to provide silk and hemp;
playing the zither
is enough to amuse myself;
what I have learned from the Master's Way
enough to bring joy to oneself.
Huí does not wish to serve."
Kǒngzǐ changed his expression gravely and said:
"Excellent!
The intention of Huí.
I have heard it said,
those who know contentment
are not burdened by profit;
those who carefully understand what they have gained for themselves
do not fear losing it;
those who cultivate themselves internally
are not ashamed even without a position.
I have recited this for a long time,
and now I see it exemplified in Huí,
this is my gain."
*Lǚshì Chūnqiū · Jìchūn Jì · Zūn Shī* Zigòng asked Kǒngzǐ, saying:
"How will later generations refer to you, Master?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"How can I be worthy of praise?
If I must say something,
it would be that I love learning and am never tired of it,
I love teaching and am never weary,
is it perhaps only this?"
*Huáinánzǐ · Yàolüè* Kǒngzǐ cultivated the Way of Chéng and Kāng,
and transmitted the teachings of the Duke of Zhōu,
to teach his seventy disciples.
He made them wear the appropriate clothing,
and study the writings,
Therefore, this is how Confucian scholars should study.
*Shuō Yuàn · Jiàn Běn*: Confucius said to Zǐlù:
"What do you like?"
Zǐlù said:
"I like long swords."
Confucius said:
"That is not what I am asking.
If you take what you are already capable of,
and add learning to it,
how far could you go!"
Zǐlù said:
"Is learning also beneficial?"
Confucius said:
"If a ruler has no ministers to remonstrate with him, he will err in government;
if a scholar has no teaching friends, he will lose virtue.
One does not release the whip from a wild horse,
nor does one remove the bow from the bow-straightening frame.
Wood straightened with a string becomes straight,
a person who accepts advice becomes wise.
Accepting learning and valuing inquiry,
who would not smoothly succeed?
To destroy benevolence and despise scholars
is close to inviting punishment.
A gentleman cannot do without learning."
Zǐlù said:
"There is bamboo on Nánshān [Southern Mountain]
that is straight without being bent;
when cut and used for shooting arrows,
penetrating rhinoceros hide.
What further learning is needed?"
Kǒngzǐ said,
"Fit it with feathers
and sharpen the arrowhead,
wouldn't its penetration be even deeper?"
Zǐlù bowed and said,
"I respectfully accept your teaching!"
*Shuō Yuàn·Jiàn Běn* Zǐlù asked Kǒngzǐ,
"May I abandon the learning of the ancients
and act according to my own ideas?"
Is that permissible?"
Kǒngzǐ said,
"No.
In the past,
the Eastern Yí admired the righteousness of the various Xià states.
There was a woman
whose husband died,
and she brought in a clandestine son-in-law
and never remarried for the rest of her life.
Not remarrying is indeed not remarrying,
but that is not the righteousness of chastity.
The younger brother of Cāngwú
married a wife who was beautiful,
and he asked to exchange her with his elder brother.
Loyalty is indeed loyalty,
but that is not propriety.
Now you want to abandon the learning of the ancients
And carrying out your intentions,
How can one know whether you're using what is wrong as right,
or using what is right as wrong?
If you do not comply from the beginning,
even if you wish to regret it,
it will be difficult!"
Zǐlù held a sword.
Kǒngzǐ asked,
"Yóu, what do you use this for?"
Zǐlù said,
"I use it to reward those who are good like the ancients,
and to defend myself against those who are bad like the ancients."
Kǒngzǐ said,
"A gentleman takes loyalty as his substance,
and benevolence as his defense.
Without stepping outside his small room,
he hears of matters a thousand *lǐ* away.
If there is evil,
he transforms bandits with loyalty,
and surrounds violence with benevolence.
Why must he carry a sword?"
Zǐlù said,
"I, Yóu, will then tuck up my robes and serve you, teacher."
Kǒngzǐ said,
"If you don't learn, how can you act?
If you don't think, how can you gain understanding?
Young ones, strive hard,
and you can become teachers of others."
*Zhōng Lùn · Xiū Běn* Confucius said:
"My disciples, strive!
Do not abandon yourselves.
If others abandon you,
how much more so if you abandon yourselves!
Those who turn away from you will be far away indeed."
*Zhōng Lùn · Xiū Běn* Confucius said to Zǐ Zhāng:

*Zhōng Lùn · Xiū Běn* Confucius said:

*Shàngshū Dàzhuàn* Confucius replied to Zǐ Zhāng, saying:
"A man marries at thirty,
and a woman marries at twenty.
A woman at twenty should be versed in the matters of weaving, silk, and spinning,
and the beauty of embroidered and patterned fabrics.
If she is not,

*Shàngshū Dàzhuàn* (Commentary on the Book of Documents) The *Book of Documents* says:
"Gāozōng was in mourning and silent;
for three years he did not speak.
What does 'mourning and silent' mean?"
The commentary says:
"Gāozōng lived in a mourning hut;
for three years he did not speak;
this is what is meant by 'mourning and silent'."
Zǐ Zhāng said:
"What was the reason for this?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"In ancient times, when the ruler passed away,
the heir-apparent would listen to the chief minister for three years at the tomb;
he would not dare to wear the late king's clothes,
nor would he assume the late king's position and listen to affairs of state there.
According to the principles of ruler and subject,
there cannot be a single day without a ruler;
there cannot be a single day without a ruler,
just as there cannot be a single day without the sky.
But considering the mourning of a filial son,
a filial son would not take up the position for three years.
Therefore, it is said:
'Duty is
that;
mourning is
this.'
To distance oneself from that and draw near to this,
then the way of a filial son is complete."
*Hán Shī Wài Zhuàn* (Han Ying's Illustrations of the Book of Poetry) 8: Zēngzǐ (曾子) committed a fault,
Zēng Xī (曾皙) took a staff and struck him with it.
He fell to the ground,
and after a while, he revived.
He rose and said:
"Master, are you perhaps unwell?"
The people of Lǔ (魯) considered Zēngzǐ virtuous,
and reported this to Fūzǐ (夫子, Confucius).
Fūzǐ (Confucius) told his disciples:
"Shēn (參)! Come here.
Have you not heard how in the past, Shùn (舜) behaved as a son?
With a small rod, he would await the light beating;
with a large staff, he would flee.
If they sought him to employ him,
he was never not by their side;
if they sought him to kill him,
he could never be found.
Now you abandon yourself to await violent anger,
standing respectfully without leaving,
not like the people of a king;
what is his crime?"
*Shuō Yuàn* (Garden of Stories) *Jiàn Běn* (Establishing the Foundation): Zēngzǐ (曾子) was weeding melons and mistakenly cut their roots.
Zēng Xī (曾皙) was angry,
and took a large staff to strike him.
Zēngzǐ (曾子) fell to the ground,
and after a while, revived.
He stood up quickly,
and stepped forward, saying:

Was it not too harsh?"
He withdrew behind a screen,
played the zither and sang,

Kǒngzǐ heard this

Do not enter."
Zēngzǐ, considering himself innocent,

When Shùn served his father,

He would endure a small beating,

Now, you entrust yourself to await violent anger,
standing there without leaving,
causing your death and trapping your father in unrighteousness.
What could be more unfilial than that?
Are you not a subject of the Son of Heaven?
What is the penalty for killing a subject of the Son of Heaven?"
what is the crime like?"
*Hán Shī Wài Zhuàn*, chapter nine. Kǒngzǐ was traveling
when he heard the sound of weeping, very sorrowful.
Kǒngzǐ said,
"Hurry, hurry,
there is a worthy person ahead." Upon arriving,
it was Gāo Yú.
Wearing coarse clothes and holding a sickle,
he was weeping by the roadside.
Kǒngzǐ stopped his carriage and spoke to him, saying,
"You do not have a bereavement,
so why do you weep so sadly?"
Gāo Yú said,
"I have lost three things:
When I was young, I studied,
and traveled among the feudal lords,
neglecting my parents,
that is the first loss;
I valued my ambition too highly,
neglecting my service to my lord,
that is the second loss;
I was close to my friends but gradually distanced myself from them,
that is the third loss.
The tree desires tranquility, but the wind never stops;
the son desires to provide for his parents, but they do not wait for him.
What goes and cannot be pursued is
Years pass;
those who depart and cannot be seen again are
one's parents.
I beg to take my leave from this."
He stood withered and died.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The disciple's warning
is sufficient to be recognized."
Thereupon, among the disciples who resigned and returned to care for their parents,
there were thirteen.
*Shuō Yuàn · Jìng Shèn* Kǒngzǐ was traveling on the road,
and heard the sound of someone crying,
the sound of which was very sad.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Drive on!
Drive on!
Ahead there is the sound of an extraordinary person."
After advancing a little,
they saw him;
it was Qiū Wúzi.
He was holding a sickle and rope, crying.
Kǒngzǐ pulled the carriage aside, got down, and asked:
"Sir, it is not as if you have suffered a bereavement,
why do you cry so sadly?"
Qiū Wúzi replied:
"I have three faults."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"I wish to hear of your three faults."
Qiū Wúzi replied,
"When I was young, I loved learning,
and traveled all over the world.
After I returned, my parents passed away,
that's one loss.
Serving my ruler with extravagance and arrogance,
my advice was not followed,
that's the second loss.
I made close friends and then broke off with them,
that's the third loss.
The tree wants to be still, but the wind doesn't stop;
the son wants to provide for his parents, but they will not wait.
What goes and does not return
is time;
what cannot be seen again
are one's parents.
Please allow me to resign from this point on."
Then he cut his own throat and died.
Kǒngzǐ said,
"Disciples, remember this,
this is enough to serve as a warning."
Thereupon, thirteen disciples returned home to care for their parents.
*Han Shi Waizhuan* 10. Tài Wáng Dǎnfù had sons,
named Tàibó, Zhòng Yōng, and Jì Lì.
Lì had a son,
named Chāng.
Tàibó knew that Tài Wáng considered Chāng worthy,
and wanted Jì to be his successor.
Tàibó went away to Wú.
When Grand Duke Tài was about to die,
he said to him:
"After I die,
you go and yield to your two elder brothers.
If they do not come,
you will be righteous and secure."
Grand Duke Tài passed away,
and Jì went to Wú to inform Bó and Zhòng.
Bó and Zhòng followed Jì and returned.
The ministers wanted Bó to establish Jì,
but Jì again yielded.
Bó said to Zhòng:
"Now the ministers want me to establish Jì,
but Jì again yields,
what should we do about it?"
Zhòng said:
"There is a principle in law,
that is to support the weak.
It is permissible to establish Jì."
Jì was then established,
and he nurtured King Wén.
King Wén indeed received the Mandate and became king.
Confucius said:
"Tàibó alone saw,
and King Jì alone knew;
Bó saw his father's will,
and Jì knew his father's heart.
Therefore, Tài Wáng, Tài Bó, and Wáng Jì,
can be said to have seen the beginning and known the end,
and were able to carry on their aspirations."
*Da Dai Li · Zeng Zi Li Xiao*
Confucius said: "If they are acceptable people,
I will bear their faults;
if they are unacceptable people,
I will decline their offenses."
The *Poetry* says:
"Having seven sons,
none comforts their mother's heart,"
this is a child's complaint.
"Rising early and sleeping late,
do not disgrace those who gave you birth,"
this speaks of not neglecting oneself.
Not being ashamed of one's parents
is the filial piety of a gentleman.
Yuèzhèng Zǐchūn descended from the hall and injured his foot.
After the injury healed,

His disciples asked,
"Master, your foot injury has healed,

Yuèzhèng Zǐchūn said,
"Good,
As for your question.

Zēngzǐ heard it from Fūzǐ, who said:

man is the greatest.
Parents give complete birth,

not to harm the body,

*Lǚshì Chūnqiū·Xiàoxíng Lǎn*. Yuèzhèng Zǐchūn went down the steps and injured his foot.
It healed, but he did not go out for several months,

Yuèzhèng Zǐchūn said:

I heard it from Zēngzǐ,
Zēngzǐ heard it from Zhòngní:
'Parents give complete birth,

Not injuring one's body,
not damaging one's form,

The superior man's conduct,
even a short step, he forgets it.
I have forgotten the Dao of filial piety,

*Da Dai Li • Zengzi Da Xiao* The Master said:
"Cutting down a tree,
killing an animal,
not according to the proper season,
is not filial piety."
*Xunzi • Zidao* Duke Āi of Lǔ asked Kǒngzǐ, saying:
"A son obeying his father's orders,
is that filial?
A subject obeying his ruler's orders,
is that loyalty?"
He asked three times,
and Kǒngzǐ did not answer.
Kǒngzǐ hurried out,
and said to Zǐgòng:
"Just now the ruler asked Qiū, saying:
'A son obeying his father's orders,
is that filial?
A subject obeying his ruler's orders,
is that loyalty?'
He asked three times and Qiū did not answer,
what do you think of that, Cì?"
Zǐ Gòng said:
"The son following the father's command is
filial;
the minister following the ruler's command is
loyal.
What response does the Master have to this?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"You are a small man!
Sì, you do not understand!
In the past, in a state of ten thousand chariots,
if there were four remonstrating ministers,
then the borders would not be diminished.
In a state of one thousand chariots,
if there were three remonstrating ministers,
then the state altars would not be endangered.
In a family owning one hundred chariots,
if there were two remonstrating retainers,
then the ancestral temples would not be destroyed.
If a father has a remonstrating son,
he will not engage in improper behavior.
If a scholar has a remonstrating friend,
he will not engage in unrighteousness.
Therefore, if a son follows his father,
how can that alone be called filial?
If a minister follows his ruler,
how can that alone be called loyal?
Examining the reason for following is what is called filial, is what is called loyal."
*Xúnzǐ · Zǐ Dào*: Zǐ Lù asked Kǒngzǐ, saying:
"If there is a person here who,
rising early and sleeping late,
plows and cultivates, plants trees,
with calloused hands and feet to support his parents,
yet does not have a reputation for filial piety,
why is that?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Could it be that his personal conduct is not respectful?
His words are not humble?
His countenance is not agreeable?
The ancients had a saying:
'The clothes are dirty, the thread is tangled,
I won't wear them.'
Now, rising early and sleeping late,
plowing and cultivating, planting trees,
with calloused hands and feet to support his parents,
if he does not have these three faults,
then how could he do this and still not have a reputation for filial piety?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Yóu, take note of this,
I will tell you.
Even if one has the strength of a national hero,
he cannot lift himself up by his own hair,
it is not that he lacks the strength,
but the situation makes it impossible.
Therefore, if at home one's conduct is not cultivated,
it is his own fault;
if when abroad one's name is not renowned,
his friend's faults.
Therefore, a virtuous person, when at home, earnestly practices filial piety;
when abroad, befriends the wise.
How can he not have the reputation of being filial?"
*Hán Shī Wài Zhuàn*, 9. Zǐ Lù said:
"If there is someone here
who rises early and sleeps late,

to serve his parents,

Kǒngzǐ said:
"I suspect is it that his person is not respectful?

The ancients had a saying:
'Is it about clothing or food?

"You toil to serve your parents,
and lack these three things,
how is it that you do not have a filial name?

"Sit!
I will tell you.
Even with the strength of a national champion,
one cannot lift oneself,
It's not that they lack the strength,
but that the situation is unfavorable.
Therefore, when a gentleman is at home, he is deeply filial;
when he is abroad, he befriends the worthy.
Why would he not have the reputation of a filial son?"
*Zhuāngzǐ, Yùyán* Zēngzǐ served twice and his heart changed twice, saying:
"When I served while my parents were alive,
three *fǔ* of grain made my heart happy;
later, when I served and received three thousand *zhōng*,
it did not reach my parents,
and my heart was sad."
A disciple asked Zhòngní, saying:
"Can someone like Shēn be said to have nothing to attach his blame to?"
Confucius said:
"He has already attached it.
For one who has nothing to attach to,
can he have sorrow?
He views three *fǔ* and three thousand *zhōng*
as watching sparrows, mosquitoes, and gadflies pass before him."
*Hán Fēizǐ, Wǔ Dù* A man of Lǔ followed his lord in battle,
and retreated in all three battles.
Zhòngní asked him the reason,
and he replied:
"I have an old father;
if I die, there will be no one to support him."
Zhòngní considered this filial piety,
and recommended him for promotion.
*Lǚshì Chūnqiū, Zhòngdōng Jì, Dāngwù* In Chǔ, there was a person named Zhígōng,
His father stole a sheep and reported it to the authorities.
The ruler arrested him and was about to execute him,
but Zhí Gōng 直躬 requested to take his place.
As he was about to be executed,

"My father stole a sheep and reported it;
isn't that honest!
My father is to be executed, and I take his place;

If someone who is both honest and filial is executed,

The King of Jīng 荊 heard of this,
and therefore did not execute him.
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 heard of this and said:
"How strange!
Zhí Gōng's 直躬 pursuit of honesty

*Xīn Xù·Zá Shì*《新序·雜事》1 Once,
Shùn 舜 himself farmed, made pottery, and fished, and personally practiced filial piety and brotherly love.
His father Gǔ Sǒu 瞽瞍 was stubborn, his mother yín 嚚 was foolish, and his younger brother Xiàng 象 was arrogant, all incorrigibly stupid.
Shùn 舜 exhausted the Way of filial piety to provide for Gǔ Sǒu 瞽瞍.
Gǔ Sǒu 瞽瞍 and Xiàng 象 plotted to dig a well and plaster a granary
in order to kill Shùn 舜.
Shùn's 舜 filial piety grew even more earnest.
When he went to the fields, he would wail and weep.
Even at fifty, he still longed for his parents like an infant.
He can be said to have been extremely filial.
Therefore, when he farmed at Mount Lì 歷,
The farmers of Mount Lìshān yielded the boundaries of their fields to each other.
When making pottery on the riverbank,
the pottery made by the potters on the riverbank was not poorly crafted.
When fishing in Thunder Lake (Léizé),
the fishermen of Thunder Lake divided their catch equally.
When he became the Son of Heaven,
the world was transformed by him,
and the barbarians all submitted willingly.
To the north, he sent out Qúsōu,
and to the south, he comforted Jiāozhǐ.
None did not admire his righteousness,
and unicorns and phoenixes appeared in the suburbs.
Therefore, Confucius said:
"The utmost of filial piety and brotherly love
extends to the spirits,
and shines upon the four seas;
this is what is meant by Shùn."
When Confucius was in his village,
he earnestly practiced filial piety.
Living in Quēdǎng,
the children of Quēdǎng, when hunting and fishing,
would give more of their catch to their relatives,
because they were transformed by his filial piety.
Therefore, the seventy-two disciples came from afar,
and submitted to his virtue.
*Shuō Yuàn·Jiànběn* Confucius said:
"In conducting oneself, there are six roots.
When the roots are established,
Then one can become a Jūnzǐ (君子, gentleman).
Establishing the body has its righteousness,
and filial piety is its foundation;
handling mourning has its propriety,
and grief is its foundation;
battle formations have their ranks,
and courage is their foundation;
governing a state has its principles,
and ability is its foundation;
residing in a state has its propriety,
and succession is its foundation;
producing wealth has its timing,
and effort is its foundation."
The Master (Fūzǐ, 夫子) also said:
"Of all human actions,
none is greater than filial piety."
Lǔ Gōng Suǒ Shì (魯公索氏), about to perform a sacrifice, lost his sacrificial animal.
Kǒngzǐ (孔子, Confucius) heard of it and said:
"Gōng Suǒ Shì (公索氏) will surely perish within three years."
He perished one year later.
A disciple asked:
"Formerly, when Gōng Suǒ Shì (公索氏) lost his sacrificial animal,
Master (Fūzǐ, 夫子) said:
'He will surely perish within three years.'
Now he has perished within a year,
how did Master (Fūzǐ, 夫子) know that he would perish?"
Kǒngzǐ (孔子, Confucius) said:
"The meaning of "sacrifice" (jì, 祭) is "seeking" (suǒ, 索).
Suǒ yě zhě,
"to exhaust,"
and it is how a filial son exhausts himself for his parents.
If even the sacrificial animal is lost at the time of sacrifice,
then what I will lose will be much more.
I know from this that he will perish."
"Garden of Stories·Distinguishing Things" Zǐ Gòng asked Confucius:
"Do the dead have knowledge or not?"
Confucius said:
"I want to say that the dead have knowledge,
but I fear that filial sons and compliant grandsons will harm the living to send off the dead.
I want to say they have no knowledge,
but I fear that unfilial sons and grandsons will abandon them unburied.
Cì, if you want to know whether the dead have knowledge or not,
you will know it yourself slowly when you die,
it's not too late."
"Garden of Stories·Returning to Simplicity" In Lǔ, there was a frugal person who
cooked food in an earthen pot.
He found it delicious after eating it,
and he served it in a clay pot,
and presented it to Confucius.
Confucius received it,
and was joyfully pleased,
as if he had received a grand sacrificial offering.
A disciple said:
"The earthen pot
is a crude vessel;
the cooked food
"It is a meager meal.
Why are you, Master, so delighted by it?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"I have heard that one who is fond of receiving admonishment thinks of his ruler,
and one who enjoys delicious food remembers his parents.
I am not delighted because the meal is sumptuous,

From *Sōushén Jì* Zēngzǐ, while following Zhòngní in Chǔ, felt a stirring in his heart.
He took leave to return home and inquire after his mother.
His mother said:

Kǒngzǐ, upon hearing this, said:

*Yùlǎn* 413, quoting *Shī Jué Shòu Xiàozǐ Zhuàn* Lǎoláizi was
a man of Chǔ,
seventy years of age,
and both his parents were still alive.

*Yùlǎn* 482 quotes *Shī Jué Shòu Xiàozǐ Zhuàn*: Zhòng Zǐ Cuī,
was the son of Zhòng Yóu. Initially,
Zǐ Lù served in Wèi.
He went to the rebellion of Kuǎi Kuì.
Hú Yǎn of Wèi was guarding the gate at the time
and killed Zǐ Lù.
When Zǐ Cuī grew up,
he told Kǒngzǐ
that he wanted to avenge his father's death.
The Master said,
"Go!"
Zǐ Cuī then went.
Yǎn knew of this and said,

*Kàng Cāngzǐ · Xùndào*: Mǐn Zǐqiān asked Zhòngní:
"How far apart are Dao and Filial Piety?"
Zhòngní said:
"Dao is
the wondrous function of nature;
Filial Piety is
the ultimate virtue of human conduct.
It encompasses and governs Heaven and Earth,
It develops all things,
and completes the myriad categories,
spreading great natural lifespans.
Its merit is supremely substantial,
yet it does not act as a storehouse for things,
nor as an office for affairs,
nor does it claim credit for its accomplishments.
If you seek it through touch and sight,
you will not be able to possess it;
it is named Dào (道).
When applied to human relationships,
it is named Xiào (孝), filial piety.
Xiào (孝),
is the name for serving one's parents well.
To serve one's parents well,
reverence and obedience are fundamental,
the intention to support them is essential.
Observe and follow their expressions,
leaving no aspect unattended to.
In uttering a single word,
in conceiving a single thought,
one dares not forget one's parents.
In moving a hand,
in placing a foot,
one dares not forget one's parents.
Serving one's ruler, one dares not be disloyal;
with friends, one dares not be untrustworthy;
when dealing with subordinates, one dares not be disrespectful;
To incline towards goodness, one dares not be lazy;
even residing in a solitary room,
one dares not relax in one's sincerity.
This is called complete filial piety.
Therefore, the utmost of perfect sincerity
penetrates to the spirits and deities,
shines upon the four seas,
and ensures that there is a response to every influence.
This is brought about by serving one's parents well.
In the past, Yú Shùn,
how greatly filial he was!
His stepmother confused his father,
and repeatedly resented and harmed him,
but Shùn's heart became even more respectful,
fearful but without resentment.
They plotted to have him dredge a well,
filling it with earth below.
At that time, Heaven's blessings stirred and moved,
and the spirits brightly protected him,
leading him out through a tunnel.
His service and care became increasingly attentive.
Consequently, his profound virtue flourished,
and he became the ruler of all under Heaven.
This was brought about by serving one's parents well.
When King Wén Wáng was the crown prince,
how greatly filial he was!
Morning and evening, he would certainly go to the outside of the sleeping quarters,
asking the eunuch,
"How is he today?"
He replied, "He is well."
The Crown Prince's expression was gently joyful.
If there was even a slight unease,
the Crown Prince's face would be filled with worry.
At every morning and evening meal,
the Crown Prince would always observe the temperature of the food;
after the meal,
he would be sure to know what dishes had been eaten.
Only then would he withdraw.
When the attendant said he was ill,
the Crown Prince would put on a solemn cap and fast,
and treat the cook's preparations
with respectful attention;
when medicine was presented,
he would personally taste it.
If the tasted food was good,
then the Crown Prince could also eat;
if the tasted food was meager,
then the Crown Prince would also not be full.
Until he recovered as before,
then everything would return to normal.
If the ruler and queen had faults,
he would gently admonish them;
what the ruler and queen loved,
even small things, he would treat with utmost reverence.
Therefore, his filial piety was complete within himself,
and his virtue spread throughout the realm.
The *Ya* section [of the *Book of Odes*] says:
"King Wén ascended and descended,
always at the Emperor's side."
This speaks of how King Wén, in his quiet actions of advancing and retreating,
was certainly aided by Heaven,
and therefore Zhòu could not harm him.
The longevity revealed in the dream of Qǐ,
the prophecy of thirty generations,
and seven hundred years,
were ordained by Heaven.
It was brought about by serving one's parents well."

"Excellent.
The way to serve one's parents
I am fortunate to have heard.
May I ask about the meaning of teaching children?"
Zhòng Ní said:
"Generally, the Three Kings taught their children,
certainly emphasizing ritual and music.
Music is used to cultivate the inner self,
ritual is used to cultivate the outer self.
When ritual and music are cultivated together,
then virtue and appearance will shine forth in countenance,
so that one can be warm, respectful, and civilized.
Now, a person who is a minister,
if sacrificing himself would benefit his lord, he should do it;
how much more so should he benefit himself in order to improve his lord?
Therefore, choose and establish loyal, good, upright, and correct men to be his teachers and mentors,
They desired that they should know the ways of father and son, ruler and minister, elder and younger.
For knowing how to be a son,
then one can be a father;
knowing how to be a minister,
then one can be a ruler;
knowing how to serve others,
then one can employ others.
This is the meaning of the Three Kings' instruction of their sons."
Mǐn Zǐqiān withdrew and served them at home.
For three years, there was no discord in the words of his parents and brothers.
His acquaintances praised his trustworthiness,
his village praised his benevolence,
and his clan praised his fraternal duty.
The reputation of his virtuous conduct
spread throughout the world.
This was brought about by his skillful service to his parents.

*Hán Shī Wài Zhuàn* 1. Duke Āi of Lǔ asked Kǒngzǐ,
"Do wise people
live long?"
Kǒngzǐ said,
"Yes.
There are three ways people die that are not due to fate;
they bring it upon themselves.
If one's living quarters are not kept in order,
one's eating and drinking is not moderate,
and one toils excessively,
illness will bring about their death.
If one is in a subordinate position but likes to interfere with superiors,
one's desires are insatiable,
and one's seeking and demanding is endless,
punishment will bring about their death.
If one uses a small force to oppose a large one,
the weak to insult the strong,
and in anger one does not consider one's strength,
weapons will bring about their death.
Therefore, there are three ways people die that are not due to fate;
are self-inflicted."
*Shuō Yuàn · Zá Yán* Duke Āi of Lǔ asked Kǒngzǐ, saying:
"Do wise men
live long?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Yes.
There are three ways in which people die that are not due to fate,
but which people bring upon themselves.
Those who do not rest and dwell at the proper times,
who are immoderate in eating and drinking,
and who indulge in excessive leisure or labor,
are killed by illness;
those who are in a lower position but offend their ruler,
and whose desires are insatiable and whose demands are unending,
are killed by punishment;
those who, being few, offend the many,
those who, being weak, insult the strong,
and those who are angry and do not consider their strength,
are killed by weapons.
These three ways of dying
are not due to fate;
people bring them upon themselves."

*Jiǎ Zǐ Xīnshū·Bǎo Fù* Kǒngzǐ said, "What is formed in youth is like one's innate nature;

*Dà Dài Lǐjì·Quàn Xué* Zǐgòng said:
"When a junzi sees a great river, he must observe it.
Why is this?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Now, water,
the junzi compares his virtue to it.
It benefits all without partiality,
resembling virtue;
those reached by it live,
those not reached by it die,
resembling benevolence;
its flowing is downward and pervasive,
even in bends and turns it follows its principle,
resembling righteousness;
its plunging into a hundred-ren ravine without hesitation,
resembling courage;
the shallow flowing through a deep abyss is unfathomable,
resembling wisdom;
it flows through weak and dangerous places,
resembling discernment;
To accept evil without resistance
, seems genuine;
To enter impure, wrapped within,
And emerge pure and clean
, seems virtuous;
Transformation is inevitable,
Measurement is always fair
, seems upright;
Fullness doesn't demand leveling
, seems strict;
It invariably breaks in the east and west
, seems intentional.
Therefore, seeing a great river, one must observe it."
*Xúnzǐ* - "Yòuzuò" Confucius watched the water flowing eastward
. Zǐ Gòng asked Confucius,
"Why is it that the superior man, upon seeing a great water, must observe it?"
What is the reason for this?
Confucius said,
"Water is great, bestowing universally upon all things without acting for itself,
resembling virtue;
Its flow descends to low places,
following its course and invariably adhering to its principle
, resembling righteousness;
Its vastness never becomes exhausted
, resembling the Way;
If something breaks its course,
its response is as swift as sound and echo
, and it doesn't fear plunging into a hundred-ren valley
Resembles courage;
its principle of measurement is invariably level,
resembles law;
being full yet not seeking to sweep over everything,
resembles uprightness;
being soft and yielding yet subtly penetrating,
resembles discernment;
moving outward and inward,
proceeding towards freshness and purity,
resembles goodness;
causing its myriad bends to invariably flow eastward,
resembles determination.
Therefore, a junzi (君子) upon seeing a great river must observe it."
*Shuō Yuàn* (說苑) *· Záyán* (雜言) Zǐgòng (子貢) asked,
"The junzi (君子) upon seeing a great river must observe it,
why is that?"
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) said,
"Water,
the junzi (君子) compares virtue to it.
It gives universally without partiality,
resembles virtue;
that which it reaches lives,
resembles benevolence;
its flow is lowly and downwards,
curves and bends all follow its principle,
resembles righteousness;
the shallow flows easily,
the deep is unfathomable,
It resembles wisdom;
Its plunging into a hundred-ren (ancient unit of length) ravine without hesitation,
resembles courage;
Being soft and weak yet subtly penetrating,
resembles discernment;
Accepting foulness without rejecting it,
resembles inclusiveness;
Entering in turbidity,
emerging clear and pure,
resembles goodness;
Its transformative power inevitably levels quantity,
resembles justice;
Being full yet not seeking to scrape together more,
resembles moderation;
Its ten thousand bends eventually leading east,
resembles intention.
Therefore, the junzi (gentleman) seeing great water must observe it."

*Xúnzǐ*, "Zǐ Dào" (The Way of a Son) Zǐ Lù, dressed in elaborate attire, went to see Kǒngzǐ.
Kǒngzǐ said,
“Yóu,
what is this affected appearance?
In the past, the Jiāng River flowed from the Mín Mountains.
When it first emerges,
its source is so small it can be scooped up with a cup.
But by the time it reaches the river's ford,
without a boat,
without avoiding the wind,
it is impossible to cross.
Is it not because the water flowing downstream is abundant?
Now your attire is so elaborate,
your countenance so full of self-importance,
who in the world would be willing to admonish you? Yóu!”
Zǐ Lù hurried out,
changed his clothes, and came back in,
appearing plain and unassuming.
Kǒngzǐ said,
“Remember this,
I will tell you.
To be flamboyant in speech is showy;
to be flamboyant in action is boastful;
to appear knowledgeable and capable outwardly
is the mark of a petty person.
Therefore, a gentleman acknowledges what he knows as knowing
and what he does not know as not knowing;
this is the essence of speech.
To acknowledge what one is capable of doing is to acknowledge it,
and to say one cannot do something when one cannot is
the ultimate in conduct.
When words are concise, one shows wisdom;
when actions are thorough, one shows benevolence.
If one is both wise and benevolent,
what more could one possibly lack!?"
*Hán Shī Wài Zhuàn*, Section 3. It is recorded that:
Zǐlù, dressed in elaborate clothing, went to see Kǒngzǐ.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Yóu,
what is this showy display?
In the past, the Jiāng River, when it flowed from its source,
in its initial stages,
was not even enough to fill a dipper.
But when it reaches the estuary of the Jiāng,
without the need for multiple boats tied together,
without concern for the wind,
it cannot be crossed.
Is it not due to the multitude of rivers that flow into it?
Now, your clothes are so elaborate,
your countenance so full of self-satisfaction,
who in the world could add to you?"
Zǐlù quickly left,
changed his clothes, and entered again,
looking subdued.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Yóu, remember this,
I will tell you.
Those who are careful with their words do not clamor,
those who are careful with their actions do not boast.
To appear knowing but actually have shortcomings,
that is the way of a petty person.
Therefore, the gentleman considers knowing to be knowing,
and not knowing to be not knowing;
this is the essence of speech.
To consider being able to be able,
and not being able to be not able;
this is the essence of action.
Being essential in speech results in wisdom,
being essential in action results in benevolence.
Having both wisdom and benevolence,
what more is there to add!"
*Shuō Yuàn · Zá Yán* (Garden of Stories · Miscellaneous Sayings). Zǐ Lù, dressed in elaborate attire, came to see Kǒngzǐ.
Kǒngzǐ said,
"Yóu,
what is all this finery?
Long ago, the Jiāng River flowed from Mount Mín,
in its beginning,
it was large enough only to float a wine cup.
But by the time it reached the Jiāng's ford,
without rafts,
without avoiding the wind,
it was impassable.
Was this not only because of the abundance of streams flowing into the lower reaches?
Now, if your clothes are so extravagant
With such overflowing appearance and demeanor,
who in the world would be willing to add anything to you!"
Zǐlù quickly went out,
changed his clothes and came back in,
now appearing natural.
Confucius said:
"Yóu, remember this,
I'll tell you.
To embellish with words
is mere showiness;
to strive through actions
is boastfulness.
A man of clever appearance, intelligence, and ability
is a petty man.
Therefore, a gentleman knows when he knows,
and admits when he doesn't know—
this is the essence of speech.
He claims ability when he has it,
and admits inability when he lacks it—
this is the perfection of action.
If speech is essential, then there is wisdom;
if action is essential, then there is benevolence.
Once you have both wisdom and benevolence,
what more could be added! Yóu!"

*Xúnzǐ 荀子, Fǎ Xíng 法行*: Zǐgòng 子貢 asked Confucius,
"Why is it that gentlemen value jade and despise min,
what is the reason?
Is it because jade is scarce and min is plentiful?"
Confucius said,
"Alas! Sì 賜,
what are you saying!
How could a gentleman value something based on its scarcity, and despise something based on its abundance!
Jade,
the junzi compares virtues to it.
Its warmth and luster,
represents rén (benevolence);
its density and texture,
represents zhì (wisdom);
its firmness and unyielding nature,
represents yì (righteousness);
its integrity without sharpness,
represents xíng (conduct);
its breaking without bending,
represents yǒng (courage);
its flaws and perfections are both visible,
represents qíng (sincerity);
when struck,
its sound is clear, resonant, and carries far,
its stopping is decisive, like words.
Therefore, even with jasper's intricate carvings,
it is not as good as jade's clear brilliance.
The *Book of Poetry* says:
'Thinking of the junzi,
his warmth is like jade.'
This is what is meant by that.
Zǐxià asked Kǒngzǐ, saying:

Kǒngzǐ said:

"What kind of person is Zǐlù?"
Kǒngzǐ said:

"What kind of person is Zǐzhāng?"
Kǒngzǐ said:

Zǐxià stepped away from his mat and asked, saying:
"In that case, why do these four gentlemen
serve you, Master?" He said:

*Lǚshì Chūnqiū · Mèng Dōng Jì · Yì Yòng* 呂氏春秋·孟冬紀·異用. When Kǒngzǐ 孔子's disciples came from afar,

*Jiǎ Zǐ Róng Jīng*. Zǐ Gòng came from his home to visit Kǒngzǐ.
Kǒngzǐ straightened his face,
raised his staff, bowed deeply, and stood, saying,
"Are your parents
perhaps not at peace?"
He put down his staff and stood, saying,
"Are your brothers
also free from illness?"
Dragging his staff, he hastened his steps down, saying,
"Are your wife and children at home
free from illness?"
Therefore, the bowing or straightening of the body,
the raising or lowering of the hands,
facial expressions, tone of voice,
each has its appropriate expression.
This is how to clarify respect and distinguish between close and distant relatives.

Xuē Jù's *Kǒngzǐ Jíyǔ* quotes from the *Xīn Xù*: Kǒngzǐ said to Zēngzǐ:

*Shuō Yuàn · Jūndào*: Duke Āi of Lǔ asked Kǒngzǐ,

"It is true."
Duke Āi asked,
"Why does he not play bó?"
Kǒngzǐ replied,
"Because it involves two dice."
Duke Āi said,
"If it involves two dice,
then why does he not play bó?"
Kǒngzǐ replied,
"Because it leads to evil ways."
Duke Āi became fearful.
After a pause, he said,
"Is it like this!
The junzi detests evil ways to such an extent!"
Kǒngzǐ replied,
"If the hatred of evil is not extreme,
then the love of good cannot be extreme either.
If the love of good is not extreme,
then the people's affection for it also cannot be extreme.
The *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says:
'Before seeing the prince,
my heart was full of sorrow;
now that I have seen him stop,
now that I have encountered him,
my heart is joyful.'
The *Shī's* love of the good way is extreme in this way."
Āigōng said,
"Excellent!
I have heard that a gentleman perfects the good in others,
and does not perfect the evil in others.
Without Kǒngzǐ,
where would I have heard these words!"
*Shuō Yuàn · Jìng Shèn* (Garden of Stories · Reverence and Caution) Yānhuí was about to travel west,
and asked Kǒngzǐ,
